idiom_name: hand-built compact JWS over OpenSSL EVP, or LibJWT's jwt_builder_* API
implementation_notes: C ships neither JOSE nor XML digital signatures, so the assertion builder is hand-written or delegated to a third-party library. Hand-written, the pattern is two functions and an opaque key handle: serialize the header and claim set as JSON, base64url-encode both segments without padding, sign the ASCII header.payload with EVP_DigestSignInit/EVP_DigestSign over an EVP_PKEY (EVP_MAC for the HMAC variant), then base64url-encode the signature into the compact form. With a dependency, LibJWT plays both roles: jwt_builder_new, jwt_builder_setkey with JWT_ALG_RS256 and a JWK, jwt_builder_claim_set and jwt_builder_time_offset for the claims, jwt_builder_generate for the token, which the caller frees. What replaces the classic structure: the AssertionBuilder class becomes an opaque key handle plus an assemble-and-sign function pair, and the only part worth keeping in your own code is the policy wrapper that pins the algorithm, the TTL and the mandatory claims.
pitfalls: Hand-rolled base64url must use the URL-safe alphabet with padding stripped; standard base64 produces segments no JOSE consumer accepts.
EVP_DigestSign needs the two-call pattern: query the signature size with a NULL output buffer first, or a fixed-size buffer silently truncates the signature (or overflows).
Ownership is split between you and the library: freeing a builder-owned buffer, or leaking the generated token on every issuance, is the standard C failure.
Key bytes read from a PEM file stay in process memory; you cannot reliably wipe them afterwards, so prefer an engine/HSM handle and keep any buffer that did hold key material short-lived.
